data.title: CUHK researchers perform city’s first robot-assisted pelvic fracture surgery
data.description:
A team of researchers from the Chinese University of Hong Kong (CUHK) has conducted the city’s first robot-assisted pelvic fracture surgery in what promises to be a safer, less intrusive alternative to a procedure typically considered among the most challenging.
CUHK’s faculty of medicine said on Friday the novel orthopaedic robotic surgical system could turn a “new page” in trauma care amid a rising number of pelvic fracture cases among the city’s rapidly ageing population.
Dr Ronald Wong Man-yeung, clinical associate professor in the CUHK’s department of orthopaedics and traumatology, said the system provided a “safe, precise, and minimally invasive” means for pelvic fracture reduction.
Wong said this could prove especially meaningful for geriatric patients, who commonly suffered from multiple medical conditions which could make traditional surgical procedures more high-risk.
“Pelvic fracture surgery is one of the most challenging surgeries or operations in orthopaedic trauma,” he said, citing the high concentration of blood vessels and vital organs surrounding the pelvis.
“So minimising the surgical trauma via minimally invasive means would then significantly reduce complications, and this robotic system, from our early experience, has shown to be a safe and efficient treatment option for these higher-risk patients.”
Pelvic fractures are a serious injury that can be life-threatening, particularly for the elderly, and have become increasingly common in Hong Kong as the city grapples with a greying population.
Complications arising from pelvic fractures can be deadly, with global research indicating that the one-year mortality rate could be as high as 15 per cent.
Wong estimated that about 2,000 people suffered from such injuries annually in Hong Kong, representing about 7 per cent of all osteoporotic fractures in the city.
The new system, which was developed in part by Beijing Jishuitan Hospital’s National Orthopaedic Medical Centre, uses real-time 3D imaging in combination with robotic arms to first realign the fracture before fixing it in place.
Since June, the university’s team has successfully used the system in three procedures at Prince of Wales Hospital in Sha Tin.
Wong said that unlike traditional open surgery, which could result in a patient losing as much as one litre of blood during the procedure, the robotic system reduced blood loss to as low as 10 to 20ml.

The reduction in surgical trauma could also improve post-operative mobilisation, recovery and pain relief for the patient, he said.
Despite the robotic system’s innovations, some limitations remained. Wong said that, for now, it was not as effective in handling fractures that had occurred more than two weeks before surgery or severe fractures affecting both sides of the pelvis.
Looking forward, the team is seeking to develop next-generation surgical technologies integrated with artificial intelligence, and has filed two provisional patents in the United States related to the developments.
In terms of deploying the robotic system more widely, Wong said the university was organising workshops to introduce it to healthcare professionals.

data.title: Embrace AI to boost competitiveness, Paul Chan says at tech festival opening
data.description:
Humanoid robots, 3D printers and artificial intelligence (AI) hubs are among the newest technologies showcased at Hong Kong’s annual electronics and technology exhibition, as the city’s finance chief encourages residents to learn how to use them.
At the opening of the four-day event on Friday, hundreds of visitors crowded the 22nd Hong Kong Computer and Communications Festival at the Convention and Exhibition Centre in Wan Chai, exploring various AI experience zones and browsing exhibitors’ products.
This year’s festival, themed “AI connect: let’s link the future,” will be hosted from August 21 to 24, featuring an “AI and digital transformation zone”.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Financial Secretary Paul Chan Mo-po said the festival focuses on the practical application and future trends of AI, which was “timely” and “highly consistent” with the direction of “AI for all”.
He said AI’s rapid advance had raised concerns over jobs, privacy, governance and security, but argued that residents who learned to use the technology effectively stood to benefit rather than be left behind.

Chan pointed to the rise of AI agents enabling “one-person companies” and even “one-person unicorns,” as individuals and small teams increasingly rely on AI to complete large projects on their own.
“If we know how to use it and use it well, AI can become a powerful tool for enhancing our capabilities and competitiveness, and create more career opportunities for us,” he said, adding that the general public should enhance their knowledge, keep studying and make good use of AI tools.
Chan also noted that the government was applying AI to public services to boost efficiency, service quality and the public’s overall experience.
He said the government’s AI efficacy enhancement team had facilitated and implemented its first batch of 30 projects, with some public services seeing significantly shorter approval or waiting times after their processes were streamlined through AI.
Among the exhibitors was Blueeyes International, which is selling 10 different models of 3D printers from mainland Chinese brand Bambu Lab, priced from HK$2,000 (US$255) to about HK$20,000.
“We want to promote the brand and let more people know that 3D printing technology has become very mature in mainland China,” said Roy Wong, Blueeyes’ sales director, adding that he still saw significant room for growth in the Hong Kong market.

As a first-time exhibitor, Wong said he expected to sell about 20 printers over the course of the event.
Also making its debut at the festival was My Robot Time, which brought about five humanoid robots to Hong Kong consumers as it looked to expand into the city.
Rita Kang, representing the company, said the robots were aimed at the K-12 education market, such as coding, and priced from HK$2,000 to HK$7,000.
She said they wanted to enhance their publicity and learn about potential customers through the festival.
Mark Li, a senior manager at On Talent Technology, showcased AI hubs, a platform that helps companies build a knowledge base, develop workflow skills, manage their information and generate meeting minutes.
It also has a portable hardware enabling cybersecurity. The hardware costs a minimum of about HK$58,000 and requires an HK$8,000-per-year licence that can serve a five- to 10-person company.
“We hope to increase the approaches to consumers and make more people know our company,” he said.
A Hong Kong resident, Bernie Concepcion, 28, said he was looking for computer parts and planned to spend about HK$200 to HK$300 at the festival.
“I initially felt a little overwhelmed [about the festival], but at the same time am excited about what is going on,” he said, adding that some keyboards and a mouse were under his consideration.

data.title: China clears Geely for landmark satellite test to spur commercial space drive
data.description:
China has approved its first private-sector commercial trial for satellite Internet of Things (IoT) services, granting a permit to a Geely-backed venture as part of broader efforts to open the country’s burgeoning satellite communications market to private capital.
The Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) granted Zhejiang Geespace Technology, the commercial space subsidiary of electric vehicle giant Geely, a two-year trial period, according to a notice published on the ministry’s website on Thursday.
Geespace will provide low-power, wide-coverage connectivity across sectors including smart transport, marine fisheries, energy, and water infrastructure.
The decision makes Geespace the first private Chinese company to secure approval for a satellite IoT commercial trial, underscoring Beijing’s push to accelerate the development of its commercial space sector.
In May, MIIT issued the country’s first satellite IoT trial permit to Beijing Guodian High-Tech Technology, an entity backed by state-owned China Mobile, the nation’s largest wireless carrier.


Satellite IoT delivers low-speed data services through satellite networks to link sensors, vehicles and equipment.
Unlike broadband constellations such as SpaceX’s Starlink or China’s state-backed Qianfan system, which focus on high-speed internet, satellite IoT prioritises reliable, low-power connections for large numbers of devices operating in remote areas without traditional network coverage, such as oceans, deserts and isolated infrastructure sites.
In its approval notice, MIIT highlighted satellite IoT as an important complement to broadband satellite services, noting that the trial would help pave the way for further private-sector participation in China’s commercial space development.
Founded in 2018, Geespace is among a growing cohort of Chinese commercial space companies deploying proprietary orbital networks.
The firm launched 64 satellites in six missions between 2022 and 2025 to complete the first phase of its network, according to its website. CEO Wang Yang told Zhejiang Daily in 2024 that the company in the long run aimed to deploy a constellation exceeding 5,600 satellites.
The domestic milestone comes as Geespace expands its global footprint. The company had conducted trials with telecoms operators in more than 20 countries across the Middle East, Africa, Southeast Asia, Central Asia, South Asia and Latin America, according to its website.
Geespace’s push into international markets puts it in direct competition with established global operators such as Iridium Communications, the US-listed market leader that has built a mature satellite IoT business over decades.
Headquartered in McLean, Virginia, Iridium is a leading global player in satellite IoT operating a 66-satellite constellation that provides voice, data and IoT connectivity services for industries including maritime, aviation, government and remote infrastructure.
The Satellite IoT market is a niche segment but expanding quickly. Research firm ABI Research estimated about 13.6 million active satellite IoT connections worldwide in 2025, up 20.7 per cent from a year earlier. That figure was projected to more than double to 28.6 million by 2030, generating roughly US$3.1 billion, according to Jake Saunders, head of the consultancy’s Asia-Pacific research division.

data.title: HKEX gold futures smash delivery record as US sanctions reshape trade
data.description:
Hong Kong Exchanges and Clearing (HKEX) has reported record-breaking physical deliveries and a trading surge in its US dollar-denominated gold futures contract, underscoring the city’s ambition to become a global hub for the precious metal amid widening trade restrictions by the United States.
The bourse operator physically delivered 145kg (319.67lbs) of gold, the highest single-day tally since the product was first launched in 2018, according to a statement published on HKEX’s official WeChat account.
The figure for Wednesday more than doubled the previous record of 63kg (138.89lbs) set in December 2018.
The surge came after HKEX relaunched the contract on July 6 – the exchange’s fourth attempt since the 1980s to establish a viable gold futures market. To boost liquidity, it introduced a marketwide waiver of its US$1-per-contract trading fee, which is scheduled to run until June 30, 2027.
Average daily trading volume reached 9,974 contracts between July 6 and August 19, with total trading value hitting US$1.35 billion. More than 30 market participants had engaged with the contract since its relaunch, according to the exchange’s statement published on Wednesday.
Gold prices rose after the US Treasury announced on the same day that it would at least double the size of its liquidity-support buy-back operations for long-dated bonds. The precious metal traded at about US$4,540 per ounce on Friday.
The HKEX milestone coincides with broader efforts to strengthen Hong Kong’s bullion ecosystem. On July 7, the city launched a trial of a centralised gold clearing and settlement system.
The measures also include Delivery Connect in partnership with the Shanghai Gold Exchange, which allows market participants to deposit physical gold holdings into a designated vault managed by the Shanghai Gold Exchange’s International Board in Hong Kong.
Separately, in late July the US Department of Homeland Security added dozens of Chinese companies to its trade blacklist, barring goods produced by those firms from entering the American market. Among the newly designated firms are three tied to China’s gold sector: Shandong Gold Mining, its subsidiary Shandong Gold Smelting Co and Xinjiang Jinchuan Mining.
Following Washington’s move, the London Bullion Market Association suspended the qualified delivery status of the targeted gold companies.
On Wednesday, the China Gold Association said the measures “lack any factual basis, violate market-oriented principles and disrupt the stability of the global gold industry chain”.

data.title: Alibaba sees payoff ahead as US$56 billion capex plan hits halfway mark
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding is expected to further accelerate cloud growth, expand operating margins and achieve faster payback on artificial intelligence investments, analysts say, as the Chinese tech giant reaches the halfway mark of its massive 380 billion yuan (US$56 billion) AI infrastructure spending plan.
“The most important incremental message, in our view, is that cloud growth has not yet peaked,” Nomura analysts said in a research note on Friday.
The comment followed Alibaba’s Thursday report of a 45 per cent revenue increase in its cloud and AI businesses for the three months ended June, marking the fastest growth in 22 quarters.
“This accelerating growth is occurring alongside meaningful margin expansion rather than at the expense of profitability,” Nomura analysts wrote, highlighting that the AI cloud unit’s adjusted Ebita margin reached 11.6 per cent, up from about 7 per cent a year ago.
Jefferies expected revenue growth for Alibaba’s Cloud and Compute Services, the company’s new reporting segment covering its cloud business and T-Head chip arm, to accelerate beyond 50 per cent year on year in the September quarter, with momentum building further into the next two quarters through March 2027.
We believe Alibaba’s results have delivered positive developments around cloud growth as a bright spot
Goldman Sachs
For the first time, the company provided clear visibility to investors on payoffs from its AI capital expenditures (capex). During an earnings call on Thursday, group CEO Eddie Wu Yongming said its AI computing investments would break even within three years – or possibly two as gross margins rose.
Wu said the company had already spent 190 billion yuan in capex as of the end of June, part of its plan announced last year to commit 380 billion yuan to digital infrastructure over the next three years.
Following the call, Goldman Sachs analysts lifted the capex estimates for its financial years 2027 and 2028 to 210 billion yuan and 240 billion yuan, respectively, driven by strong AI demand and favourable return on invested capital (ROIC) that prompted elevated spending.
“We believe Alibaba’s results have delivered positive developments around cloud growth as a bright spot, higher certainty on ROIC despite capex uplift, and an inflection in earnings per share growth with improving quick commerce unit economics,” Goldman Sachs said.
Shares of Alibaba, which owns the South China Morning Post, fell 2.5 per cent to close at HK$123 in Hong Kong on Friday.
While its 67.7 billion yuan quarterly outlay eclipsed the 52.8 billion yuan spent by domestic peer Tencent Holdings, the figures underscore a divergence in scale compared with US hyperscalers.
Major American tech giants – Amazon.com, Microsoft, Alphabet and Meta Platforms – are collectively projected to spend around US$700 billion on capital expenditure in 2026, averaging US$44 billion per quarter per company.
One of Alibaba’s biggest financial concerns remains the increasing cash outflow under its aggressive spending plan. Free cash outflow in the June quarter more than doubled to 44.7 billion yuan year on year, as heavier investment in cloud infrastructure strained cash generation.
Analysts forecast that surging demand for compute and the deployment of proprietary AI chips would offset short-term cash flow pressures.
Wu also justified the spike in quarterly capex, citing procurement timing, additional central processing unit capacity to meet AI agent demand, and higher chip prices.
Wu offered a telling example of strong demand: Nvidia’s A100 cards purchased in 2020 and V100 cards purchased in 2018 were still running at full capacity in its data centres.
A central pillar of this return profile is Alibaba’s proprietary chipmaking arm, T-Head. Having shipped more than 500,000 units of its previous-generation chips cumulatively, Alibaba began commercialising T-Head’s latest Zhenwu M890 chips on its cloud in supernode form – designed to knit hundreds or thousands of chips together to act as one giant supercomputer – earlier this month.
Looking ahead, Wu said long-term revenue growth and margin expansion trends would be “exceptionally strong”, and as a result, the cloud unit was “highly confident” in its ability to achieve the goal of US$100 billion in external revenue by 2030.

data.title: Opatra London and Hong Kong distributor suspend local operations after arrests
data.description:
The British headquarters and Hong Kong distributor of beauty product company Opatra London have suspended local operations after allegations of aggressive sales tactics triggered the arrest of local senior staff and a raid on a corporate secretarial office in Sheung Wan.
In a statement issued on Friday, Opatra London continued to distance itself from the local distributor, which it said owned and operated the local stores independently.
The office of the local company, Sayles Retail, was raided by customs officers on Tuesday, and they arrested its financial and administration managers under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance the following day.
“Opatra London confirms that, by mutual agreement with its local distributor, the Hong Kong distribution agreement has been suspended,” the company said. “The Opatra-branded stores in Hong Kong are independently owned and operated by a local distributor.”
The London office said Hong Kong was an important market for the group and its commitment to the city’s customers remained unchanged.

data.title: MTR Corp senior manager conned out of HK$74m by fraudster posing as HSBC UK staff
data.description:
A senior manager at Hong Kong rail giant the MTR Corporation was allegedly conned out of HK$74 million (US$9.4 million) in a two-year-long scam by a fraudster posing as an employee of HSBC UK who lured the victim into investing in green bonds.
Police said on Friday they had received a report from a 59-year-old man who claimed he had been scammed. The case has been classified as obtaining property by deception, and no arrests have been made.
“The victim said he received a phone call from a scammer claiming to be an HSBC UK employee, who lured him into investing in green bonds,” the force said.
Following the scammer’s instructions, the victim made 12 transfers totalling about HK$74 million to designated overseas bank accounts – including an account at Barclays Bank in the United Kingdom – between February 2024 and January this year.
“The victim subsequently failed to recover the funds, suspected he had been scammed, and reported the case,” police said.

A police source said the victim was a senior manager at the MTR Corp and that the scammer had used the Barclays Bank account to receive the money.
Hong Kong has recently been hit by a series of high-profile scams. Last month, a woman lost nearly HK$69 million in a month-long fraud in which scammers posed as mainland Chinese officials.
The 43-year-old woman received calls from people claiming to be mainland officers, who accused her of committing a crime and demanded money to prove her innocence.
The victim transferred about HK$68.9 million to designated bank accounts in multiple transactions between July 2 and August 1.

data.title: Evergrande’s fine, China cuts US Treasury holdings: the numbers moving markets
data.description:
While investors saw Beijing’s holdings of US government debt shrink and US Treasuries yield rise, a life sentence for China Evergrande Group founder Hui Ka-yan marked a symbolic end to an era of breakneck expansion in the country’s property sector.
Here are some of the figures that have drawn the most market attention this week.
An 8.82 billion yuan fine for Hui Ka-yan’s Evergrande

A Shenzhen court sentenced China Evergrande Group founder and former chairman Hui Ka-yan, also known as Xu Jiayin, to life imprisonment for “multiple combined crimes” on Thursday, while ordering the confiscation of all his personal property.
Evergrande was fined 8.82 billion yuan (US$1.31 billion), while its onshore operating unit Hengda Real Estate received a separate 7 billion yuan fine. The penalties were among the largest corporate fines imposed by a Chinese court for criminal offences.
China’s US Treasury holdings hit 18-year low

China reduced its holdings of US Treasuries to US$633.4 billion in June, the lowest level in nearly 18 years, as Beijing continued to diversify its foreign-exchange reserves amid geopolitical tensions and uncertainty over the US policy outlook.
The retreat came into sharper focus this week as a sell-off pushed long-dated US Treasury yields to multi-year highs. The 30-year yield climbed more than 4 basis points to 5.31 per cent on Monday, its highest since June 2007, while the benchmark 10-year yield rose more than 2 basis points to 4.724 per cent.
CXMT’s market value tops 4 trillion yuan

CXMT, China’s leading dynamic random-access memory (DRAM) maker, saw its market value surge to 4.13 trillion yuan (US$612 billion) on Monday, becoming China’s most valuable listed company amid an AI-fuelled rally in memory-chip stocks.
The Hefei-based chipmaker briefly overtook Tencent Holdings last week to become China’s most valuable listed company, highlighting investors’ enthusiasm for semiconductor companies benefiting from booming AI-related memory demand.
Fifty-eight per cent of Hong Kong’s wealthy expect to work beyond retirement

More than half of Hong Kong’s high-net-worth individuals expect to continue working beyond the traditional retirement age, suggesting that the city’s wealthy are increasingly planning their finances around longer working lives.
Some 58 per cent said they expected to work past retirement age, according to a Manulife survey. Of those surveyed, 32 per cent expected to work for another five to 10 years, while 26 per cent said they planned to keep working for as long as possible.
Unitree Robotics sees 629 per cent surge on debut

Shares of Unitree Robotics surged 629 per cent above their initial public offering price to open at 1,100 yuan in their Shanghai debut on Wednesday, briefly valuing China’s best-known humanoid robot maker at about 445 billion yuan.

data.title: Dog that fatally bit handler at Hong Kong pet centre a stray awaiting adoption
data.description:
A dog that fatally mauled its handler at a Hong Kong pet training facility was a stray awaiting adoption, the South China Morning Post has learned, with residents living nearby saying they were not worried as the animals at the centre were kept indoors.
A check by the SCMP on Friday morning found Pawsgate pet training centre at Ping Yeung Tsuen in Ta Kwu Ling closed a day after the attack. But staff members returned to the facility in the early afternoon to pick up three dogs, with three remaining.
According to a source familiar with the facility, the dog involved in the attack on Wong Choi-yi, the 33-year-old owner of Pawsgate, is one year and four months old. It is a brown mixed-breed weighing 30kg, which could have pit bull ancestry – a type banned from import and breeding in Hong Kong.
The dog was a stray that had previously been cared for at a car park on Lok Ma Chau Road, but was left without a home when the site closed in April.
It was taken in by a dog volunteer and a shelter, before being transferred to Wong’s training centre and pet hotel on August 11 and put up for adoption.
Police earlier identified Pawsgate as a facility located at 111 Ping Yeung Tsuen, with a 4,500 sq ft grass lawn, a dog swimming pool, indoor play areas and dog boarding and training services.
According to the source, the centre started operations in January this year, run by Wong and a 41-year-old partner surnamed Cheung.

The facility was shut and locked on Friday morning, with two vehicles parked inside the gates but with no staff in sight.
Surrounded by thick scrub, Pawsgate sits on a small, quiet road that is not commonly used by residents living in the villages of Ta Kwu Ling.
A resident surnamed Leung said she had never been worried about the dogs at the facility as she had never seen them being let out.
However, after the incident, she said she would be “more careful about my children’s safety”.
Another resident, a retiree and dog owner surnamed Li, was surprised to hear about the incident.
“I do not understand how it happened. I have never heard of dogs killing people,” he said.
Despite the incident, he said he was not unduly alarmed as the training centre kept its animals indoors. He added that he rarely noticed unleashed or stray dogs in the area, and those that he did see were generally docile.

A logistics worker employed nearby, who gave his name only as Mic, was troubled by the incident, saying he was worried that the dogs could escape and attack people in the neighbourhood.
“Many children pass through this area, and it’s a residential zone, so parents need to be careful. There are also lots of rubbish collection points where dogs can come scavenging for food,” he said.
Mic had not known that the training centre and pet hotel existed, and had not previously heard dogs barking in the area.
“It’s quite ironic that a dog hotel owner was killed by a dog she was looking after. Is this really a suitable place to run such a business?” he said.

data.title: Ex-Deloitte IT manager jailed for 22 months over HK$1.2 million laptop theft
data.description:
A former Deloitte information technology manager has been jailed for 22 months for stealing 423 laptops worth HK$1.2 million (US$153,000) from the accounting firm’s Hong Kong office to fund his stock trading addiction.
The District Court sentenced Ho Man-kit, 40, on Friday after he pleaded guilty earlier this month to a count of theft for misappropriating Lenovo computers and selling them to an electronics recycler between September 2021 and February 2023.
Deputy Judge Minnie Wat Lai-man said the defendant had abused his employer’s trust over a long period and was unable to compensate the company because he had lost all the illegal proceeds through unsuccessful stock trading.
But Wat found reasons to impose a lighter sentence, highlighting Ho’s willingness to take responsibility, his difficulties in finding a new job due to mental health issues and the limited impact the case had on Deloitte’s reputation.
She also noted that the defendant was unlikely to reoffend and had strong support from family members who persuaded him not to commit suicide after the offence came to light.
The offence came to light after an IT engineer discovered a shortfall of 399 laptops at Deloitte’s office at Cityplaza in Quarry Bay on February 13, 2023.
The engineer and an administrative officer reviewed live surveillance footage and found that the defendant, who was supposedly on leave, had attempted to sell a box of 15 laptops to a recycler at around 7.30pm on the same day. The pair immediately intervened to call off the transaction.
Ho confessed his wrongdoing to his supervisor at a meeting two days later and surrendered himself to police that afternoon.
A detective constable later recovered 24 other Deloitte laptops from the recycler’s premises at Sin Tat Plaza in Mong Kok.
According to the recycler’s owner, the defendant said Deloitte had allowed him to sell the laptops, which he claimed were either outdated or bought by mistake.
Bank records showed that Ho had received more than HK$458,000 from the illicit sales. The defendant claimed that he had also received cash from the recycler for the transactions.
Defence counsel said in mitigation that Ho was under significant family-related stress. His wife experienced postnatal depression, while his ailing father underwent surgery for lung cancer.
Theft is punishable by up to 10 years’ imprisonment, but the maximum is seven years when the case is heard in the District Court.

data.title: Chinese court accepts Evergrande liquidation 1 day after founder’s sentence
data.description:
A court in southern China’s Guangdong province formally accepted a bankruptcy liquidation petition against China Evergrande Group’s main onshore unit, closing the final chapter in the unravelling of what was once the country’s largest property developer.
The Guangzhou Intermediate People’s Court said on Friday that Guangzhou Rural Commercial Bank’s Huaxia branch met the legal criteria under the nation’s Enterprise Bankruptcy Law to force the Evergrande unit, Hengda Real Estate, into liquidation, citing the firm’s inability to pay mature debts and insufficient total assets.
The decision came just a day after the Shenzhen Intermediate People’s Court handed down a life sentence to Hui Ka-yan, the billionaire founder also known as Xu Jiayin, following a high-profile trial over financial fraud and mismanagement.
Hui was convicted on multiple financial charges, stripped of his political rights for life and ordered to forfeit all personal property.
The Shenzhen court also levied administrative fines totalling 8.82 billion yuan (US$1.32 billion) on parent company China Evergrande Group and 7 billion yuan on Evergrande Real Estate, alongside orders to recover remaining illegal gains.
The rapid sequence of events underscores Beijing’s determination to bring a definitive end to the years-long debt crisis surrounding Evergrande. Once the poster child of China’s debt-fuelled property boom, the company spiralled into crisis in 2021 after falling foul of Beijing’s “three red lines” – regulatory curbs on overleveraged developers.
Its subsequent default on more than US$300 billion in total liabilities sent shock waves through the world’s second-largest economy, triggering a systemic property downturn, widespread homebuyer protests over unfinished flats and a Hong Kong liquidation order against its offshore holding company in early 2024.

The liquidation filing coincided with broader structural overhauls to China’s insolvency framework, with China’s top legislative body signalling potential shifts in how corporate restructurings will be handled moving forward.
Speaking at a press conference on Friday, Huang Haihua, spokesman for the Legislative Affairs Commission of the National People’s Congress Standing Committee, detailed proposed revisions to the nation’s Enterprise Bankruptcy Law.
The draft amendments aim to strengthen temporary protection mechanisms to safeguard restructuring procedures, clarify filing criteria for creditors and debtors, and mandate strict information disclosure standards during corporate reorganisations.
Notably, the proposed legislation also aims to enhance cross-border bankruptcy rules, clarifying Chinese courts’ jurisdiction over international insolvency cases. The legal reform is scheduled for its second reading from August 25 to 28.

data.title: Henderson Land posts 66% profit surge after run of strong sales
data.description:
Henderson Land Development, one of Hong Kong’s largest developers, reported a 66 per cent rise in its interim profit for the first half of the year following a strong run of property sales, according to its filing with the Hong Kong stock exchange on Thursday.
The developer, controlled by the family of its late founder Lee Shau-kee, said its unaudited underlying profit attributable to equity shareholders had reached HK$5.07 billion (US$646 million) for the January to June period, up HK$2.02 billion from a year earlier.
Henderson Land declared an interim dividend of 50 HK cents per share, unchanged from the same period last year, which will be distributed on September 17.
“During the first half of 2026, the group successfully capitalised on favourable market conditions to launch a number of urban projects for sales,” said co-chairmen Peter Lee Ka-kit and Martin Lee Ka-shing in the filing.
Recent launches included batches of properties at developments including Chester and One Victoria Cove in Hung Hom, Highwood in Ma Tau Kok, and Victoria Voyage in Kai Tak, they said.
More than 90 per cent of the flats at Chester had been sold by the end of June, while all 468 residential units available in the first three rounds of sales at One Victoria Cove had sold out, the executives added.
Along with sales of other projects, the group’s attributable contracted sales in Hong Kong had surged 188 per cent to HK$18.11 billion in the first half, according to the company.
Meanwhile, about HK$17.06 billion had yet to be recognised as revenue from sales, the group said.
In the second half of the year, Henderson Land planned to launch eight development projects with a combined 3,400 homes in Hong Kong, including the developer’s remaining stock, it said.
“Despite the ongoing Middle East war and disrupted oil shipping routes, Hong Kong’s economic fundamentals remain stable,” the co-chairmen said.

Hong Kong’s creation of its first five-year plan for the 2026-2030 period would also help the city “better integrate into and serve the overall national development, thereby fostering long-term economic growth”, they added.
As for the firm’s office portfolio, Henderson said its premium projects in Central had benefited from the “flight-to-quality trend among tenants in the finance, insurance and legal sectors”, which “drove the vacancy rate of office developments in core Central to its lowest level in nearly two years”.
As of June, The Henderson – a 465,000 sq ft prime office development in Central – had achieved a leasing rate of over 90 per cent. Its tenants included Point72, Christie’s, Carlyle, Audemars Piguet and Cohen & Steers, according to the company.
Henderson’s other office projects also had an occupancy rate of about 90 per cent, while the first phase of Central Yards – the 1.6 million sq ft mixed-use development on the New Central Harbourfront – was set to be completed in late 2026 and open in 2027, it added.
Jane Street Asia will serve as the anchor tenant for Central Yards, with the US-based quant trading firm leasing 223,437 sq ft in the building for HK$137 per square foot per month, or HK$30.6 million per month, excluding fees, making it one of the largest leasing transactions in Central in recent years.
“The remaining areas are attracting strong interest from leading multinational companies,” the group said. “During the first half of 2026, a joint venture company of the group successfully secured a five-year tenancy for the Central Harbourfront Event Space adjacent to Central Yards.”

data.title: Chinese AI firms forced to optimise software as local chips trail Nvidia’s
data.description:
Chinese AI companies are optimising software to cope with surging demand for inference, as part of that workload still relies on computing power from a limited pool of high-end chips amid restricted access to Nvidia processors.
Compared with training an artificial intelligence model, which relies on high-end chips, inference – a later phase in which the trained model applies its knowledge to process responses – can be adapted to domestic hardware. However, industry insiders said complex tasks like coding still required Nvidia chips, which meant the sector was facing acute compute constraints as AI moved from model development to large-scale deployment.
“The demand side is now showing a bipolarisation,” said Guan Jiawei, vice-president of inference optimisation start-up Approaching.AI, noting that demand for high-quality tokens – the basic units of data that models process and generate – far outstripped supply.
High-tier tasks required stringent performance metrics that domestic processors could not yet reliably deliver, Guan said, adding that advanced Chinese models “place high demands on chips … especially in scenarios like coding, where users are willing to pay a premium”.
“If we rely solely on domestic chips for inference, they can only handle the low-quality tier – the tier with weak demand and weak monetisation,” Guan said. “That makes it very hard to find a viable commercial path. That’s why high-quality tokens still depend on Nvidia.”
Skyrocketing token usage, as AI turns more agentic – performing real-world tasks rather than just answering questions – has exacerbated the compute squeeze. China’s average daily token calls exceeded 140 trillion in March, up more than 1,000-fold from the beginning of 2024, according to the National Data Administration.


The pressure on computing supply is also reflected in chip prices. Monthly rental prices for Nvidia H200 chips surged above 100,000 yuan (US$14,857) earlier this year, from 50,000 yuan to 80,000 yuan by the end of the third quarter last year, according to data from Approaching.AI.
“If we continue to rely on the same inference technology, the growth in token demand would require an impossible amount of computing capacity,” Guan said. “Based on this calculation, China could need around 300,000 high-end chips for inference in 2026 and as many as 300 million by 2030. That is clearly not realistic.”
In response, Chinese firms have had to think outside the box.
To give one example, Moonshot has designed a data transmission library for heterogeneous inference scenarios in which different chips work together. The system “enables efficient data exchange” between Nvidia H20 and Huawei Technologies Ascend 910B chips, according to the project’s website.
Similar to Moonshot, Approaching.AI has turned to a technique known as heterogeneous P/D disaggregation, which allows different chips to handle different parts of the same AI task. Huawei’s Ascend 910B chips can handle the initial processing of a request, while Nvidia’s H20 chips generate the response, with software transferring the information between the two.
Approaching.AI said its inference engine, KTransformers, had been used to run DeepSeek’s full-size model on a single Nvidia RTX 4090 graphics processing unit combined with a central processing unit and large amounts of memory. It said the approach could reduce the cost of running the model by 10 to 20 times.
The approach appears to be paying off, with the start-up saying its revenue in June surpassed its total revenue for all of last year.

data.title: Hong Kong Tiananmen vigil organiser, former leaders guilty of inciting subversion
data.description:
A now-disbanded alliance behind Hong Kong’s annual Tiananmen Square vigil, along with two of its former leaders, have been found guilty of inciting subversion under the national security law for advocating an end to “one-party dictatorship” in mainland China.
The Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, its former chairman Lee Cheuk-yan and former vice-chairwoman Chow Hang-tung were convicted at West Kowloon Court on Friday over one of the group’s operational objectives, which it said was intended to promote democracy and human rights.
Former lawmaker Lee and Chow, a barrister, have been remanded in custody for nearly five years. A fourth defendant, former vice-chairman Albert Ho Chun-yan, has also been detained for more than four years and is awaiting sentencing after pleading guilty to the offence in January.
Three High Court judges presiding over the high-profile trial were tasked with determining whether the alliance’s objective of ending one-party rule on the mainland violated the Chinese constitution, which guarantees the Communist Party’s leadership.
Prosecutors argued that Article 1 of the constitution barred anyone from overthrowing the leadership of the Communist Party of China, which they said was the “defining feature of socialism with Chinese characteristics”.
They alleged that the defendants fostered public hatred towards Beijing through “objectively negative” portrayals, inciting others to overthrow the central government under the pretext of promoting democracy and commemorating the Tiananmen Square crackdown in Beijing on June 4, 1989.

The prosecution said the alliance’s operation of the June 4 museum, publication of periodicals and organisation of annual events — including the city’s annual candlelight vigil and the cleaning of the Pillar of Shame sculpture — were intended to “promote and spread” the group and its illegal stance.
The defence contended that all the alliance’s objectives, which also included vindicating the 1989 movement and building a democratic China, were a legitimate exercise of fundamental human rights.
Lee testified that he did not oppose Communist Party rule on the mainland but said the one-party system was incompatible with the constitution’s preamble, which provides for “multiparty cooperation and political consultation” under the party’s leadership.
Chow argued that advocating an end to one-party rule was not the same as seeking to oust the party from its leading position. She added that pursuing democratic change in society should not be considered illegal in the first place.
Set up after the 1989 crackdown, the alliance organised annual candlelight vigils at Hong Kong’s Victoria Park to mark the incident and call for accountability and sweeping political reforms across the border.
The event had been the only large-scale commemoration of the Tiananmen Square crackdown held on Chinese soil.
Police prohibited the vigil for the first time in 2020 on public health grounds related to the Covid-19 pandemic. The 2021 event was banned for similar reasons before the alliance disbanded in September that year.
Prosecutors stressed that the trial was not politically motivated and was not designed to punish dissidents, “even though the evidence shows the defendants’ incitement was committed in the name of so-called democracy or the June Fourth incident – combining negative information targeting the state”.
Inciting subversion carries a maximum sentence of 10 years’ imprisonment under the national security law.

data.title: Hong Kong financiers press for tax breaks after Singapore’s challenge
data.description:
Hong Kong should press ahead with its proposed tax break on carried interest, the performance fees earned by hedge fund and private equity managers, after Singapore unveiled a rival tax-exemption scheme, according to industry participants.
The bill, submitted to lawmakers in June and expected to come to a vote later this year, has sparked debate in the financial industry. Some participants argue that the exemption is too narrow in scope, while others question the fairness of exempting ultra-wealthy fund managers from tax.
Bankers and other financial professionals have voiced concern that traders could relocate to rival jurisdictions offering similar tax incentives if the bill were delayed, and in this context, Singapore’s move was widely seen as a challenge.
“Hong Kong needs to proceed quickly with the proposed law change to continue strengthening our established reputable position as the No 1 global wealth management centre,” said Jasmine Lee Shun-yi, vice-president of Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants, adding that Singapore had taken action to “try to match our bill”.
“The tax break will be vital for Hong Kong to further increase its competitiveness to attract global fund managers to establish the entirety of their businesses in Hong Kong. In conjunction, it will also attract relevant diverse talent to consider moving to Hong Kong as well.”
Lee is optimistic about the potential benefits of the new bill.
“Many of these fund managers work and live in many different markets, and they make their decisions of choosing the places of residency very carefully,” she said. “If they choose to stay in Hong Kong to enjoy this tax break, they will benefit the city with their various spending, such as buying properties and paying for their children’s education. These will benefit the local real economy.”
Hong Kong needs to proceed quickly with the proposed law change to continue strengthening our established reputable position
Jasmine Lee, Hong Kong Institute of Certified Public Accountants
At present, Singapore’s top personal income tax is 24 per cent, and the UK’s is 45 per cent. The US federal top rate is 37 per cent, though combined federal and state taxes can exceed 50 per cent in high-tax states such as California and New York. Corporate tax follows a similar pattern: 17 per cent in Singapore, 25 per cent in the UK, and 21 per cent in the US.
By contrast, in Hong Kong, the salaries tax is capped at a standard rate of 15 per cent, while the corporate profit tax is 16.5 per cent.
Under the proposal, fund employees would be exempt from salaries tax on performance fee income, and fund houses would not need to pay profit tax on such income. The changes would take effect retroactively from April 2025, according to a government paper presented to lawmakers earlier this year.
According to the paper, the exemption would give Hong Kong the world’s lowest tax rate for managers of hedge funds, private equity funds and venture capital funds whose income is largely performance-based.
That edge is now being tested by Singapore.

The ‌Monetary Authority of Singapore and the city’s finance ministry on Wednesday announced a package of measures, including a tax exemption for investment profits earned by managers of single family offices and other qualifying funds.
“The newly announced measures are expected to reinforce Singapore’s position as a leading asset management hub,” said Anulekha Samant, partner and co-head of real estate and asset management for tax at KPMG in Singapore.
Samant said that profit-related tax exemptions aligned with professional pay to help attract global talent, while hedge fund initiatives signalled a clear push to deepen market activity and attract firms to Singapore.
A spokesman for Hong Kong’s Financial Services and the Treasury Bureau said the city’s bill would widen the definition of qualifying funds to include pension funds, endowment funds and single-investor “funds-of-one”, while extending the scope of qualifying investments to cover loans, private credit, digital assets and precious metals.
Clause-by-clause scrutiny of the bill in the Legislative Council’s Bills Committee had been completed, he added, with the government aiming to resume the second reading debate in the second half of this year.
“A number of fund management companies, both local and overseas, have expressed interest in establishing a presence or expanding their operations in Hong Kong, in regard to the tax incentives proposed in the bill,” the spokesman said.
However, Hong Kong representatives said that tax policy was only one part of a broader, established ecosystem.
“Hong Kong’s position as Asia’s premier asset management hub is not built on a single tax incentive, but on an unrivalled ecosystem of access, rule of law and long-term certainty,” said Rocky Tung Yat-ngok, executive director of Hong Kong’s Financial Services Development Council.
Levelling the playing field on incentives highlighted Hong Kong’s core strengths, with its “deep capital pool” and “unique access to emerging opportunities” in mainland China positioning the city for continued leadership, he added.
Market observers echoed this view, noting that while tax breaks were effective lures, they were only part of the broader equation for global capital.
Hong Kong’s position as Asia’s premier asset management hub is not built on a single tax incentive, but on an unrivalled ecosystem
Rocky Tung Yat-ngok, Financial Services Development Council
“Tax alone is not the decisive factor,” said Kenny Tang Sing-hing, chairman of the Hong Kong Institute of Financial Analysts and Professional Commentators. “Fund managers ultimately weigh market depth, liquidity, and the diversity of financial products when deciding where to anchor their headquarters.”
Tang added that Hong Kong held a clear edge in these areas, adding that its growing range of offshore yuan products would further bolster the city’s appeal to international investors.
Assets under management in Hong Kong’s asset and wealth-management industry rose 20 per cent year on year to a record HK$42.2 trillion (US$5.4 trillion) in 2025, with net fund inflows surging 193 per cent to HK$2.1 trillion, official data showed.

data.title: Hong Kong beauty sector faces new claims of hard-sell tactics and abuse
data.description:
More consumers in Hong Kong have come forward to allege aggressive sales tactics across the beauty sector, including credit card abuse, unwanted physical contact and pressure to buy costly products, on the back of a crackdown on the local operations of a UK-based brand.
Legal experts warned that such practices could breach the Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which prohibits harassment, coercion and misleading conduct used to pressure consumers into making purchases they otherwise would not have made.
Non-consensual physical contact could also trigger additional criminal liability, they added.
Following the arrest of two managers at the Hong Kong operator of UK-based beauty chain Opatra London over coercive sales practices, at least one top executive has resigned, while customs officers continue investigating six customer complaints involving disputed sums between HK$1,800 and HK$100,000.
The brand’s four Hong Kong branches – two in Sha Tin, one in Yuen Long and one in Causeway Bay – have since suspended operations.
Now, more victims have detailed alleged aggressive sales tactics they have encountered while shopping for beauty products.
For 22-year-old university student John Cheung*, it took just a few seconds to be dragged into what he described as a “beauty trap” on the busy Hankow Road in Tsim Sha Tsui in May.
Outside a Lionesse shop, Cheung said he was approached by a saleswoman who handed him a “free sample”.
He said the woman told him he had “dark eye circles” before applying an unidentified skincare product directly to his face. Concerned about a possible skin reaction and caught off guard by the ambush, he agreed to enter the shop.
Once he was seated, Cheung said staff applied another liquid, claiming it was a HK$1,560 deep cleanser. They then showed him the “dirt” removed from his skin in a mirror in an attempt to persuade him to buy the product.
After he agreed, Cheung said he was hurried into signing an electronic form, with the signature box enlarged to the point that he could not read the contract terms, including a “no refunds” clause.
Instead of handing over the product, Cheung said the saleswoman then directed him to a free facial and bombarded him with questions about his age and employment status, along with two other staff members.
Under pressure, Cheung said he agreed to purchase a HK$30,000 annual facial package, but explicitly requested an instalment plan capped at HK$2,500 a month due to his credit card limit.
Cheung said one of the salesmen took his card and made multiple attempts to process transactions exceeding HK$2,500.
Bank records showed five unsuccessful attempts, he said, for HK$30,000, HK$8,440, HK$5,000, HK$7,500 and, finally, HK$2,500. He said the bank immediately blocked the card because of the suspicious activity.
Cheung said he ultimately paid HK$2,500 via PayMe to a merchant named “Vertex Innovations Limited” so he could leave the shop.
When he sought a refund through the Consumer Council, Cheung said Lionesse’s management denied allegations of high-pressure sales practices, arguing that the open shop environment meant he could have “left immediately”.
The company said the failed transaction records reflected standard authorisation procedures between the bank system and the merchant terminal and did not constitute improper sales practices. It declined to provide a refund, instead offering to exchange products of the same value.
In response to queries from the South China Morning Post, Apex Retail, which manages Lionesse in Hong Kong, declined to comment on individual allegations or circumstances that did not involve identifiable customer matters.
Recalling the experience, Cheung said: “I’m just a student. The incident put immense psychological pressure on me and forced me to waste a lot of time organising bank records, payment details and relevant documents to file a complaint.”
He added: “I never intended to get involved in beauty services, but this experience made me realise how dark and manipulative beauty sales could be.”
He is now seeking a chargeback of HK$4,060 from the bank.
Company registration records show the directors of Apex are Ozel Barnos, Eli Vaknin, Sagi Vardi, Yogev Itzhak Vardi and Yinon Avraham Vardi.
The company website, which has become inaccessible, said it started as an Israeli family business and now had about a dozen shops in the city, under the brands of Earth, Napara, Privilege Boutique, Avinichi, Dualsonic and more.
Another firm to come under scrutiny was The Mineral Boutique, a brand under Beauty Express Group that has at least five branches in major shopping centres.
A 42-year-old clerk surnamed Wong alleged that similar tactics were used when a saleswoman applied a product directly onto her skin without permission at the Log-on shop in Festival Walk, Kowloon Tong, in June.
Wong said the saleswoman claimed the product could only be removed using a specialised device inside the counter area.
Once inside, Wong alleged, staff repeatedly grabbed her hand when she tried to pull away and cornered her while attempting to sell her high-value products, alongside a store manager.
When Wong attempted to leave, she said the saleswoman replied: “What is there left to think about? You’ve already seen the results.”
Wong said the remark prompted her to leave immediately and then file a formal complaint with City’super, the parent company of Log-on.
In a response to Wong, City’super said it had investigated the incident, reiterated that aggressive sales tactics were strictly prohibited, and offered her a gift box.
City’super told the SCMP that it had received two customer “comments” about the counter’s services in the past year, as well as “a limited number of comments or complaints” over the past five years.
It said all cases had been investigated and handled through established procedures.
Asked whether such complaints influenced lease renewals, City’super declined to comment on specific contractual arrangements.
“We evaluate business relationships and commercial arrangements based on a range of factors including compliance with applicable laws and regulations, operational requirements, customer feedback and other relevant considerations,” it said.
Beauty Express Group declined to comment on the complaint, citing a lack of sufficient information to identify the customers involved.
It told the SCMP that it did not tolerate aggressive sales practices, non-consensual physical contact, or any conduct that compromised a customer’s ability to make a free and informed purchasing decision.
The group’s directors include Aviad Ben Ezra and Baruch Szerer. Other brands under the group include Telosin, Premier by Dead Sea, Gratiae and more.

Lawyer Eric Chan Pak-ho said the tactics used on the student could constitute an offence under the Trade Descriptions Ordinance. However, the key question was whether sales staff had used “harassment, coercion or undue influence” to persuade Cheung to agree to each purchase.
Chan added that concealing no-refund policies could increase the company’s legal liability.
Under the law, practices that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice or conduct, and cause them to make a purchase they would not otherwise have made, are considered an offence.
Commercial lawyer Kenix Yuen Pui-kwan said that applying beauty products to a consumer’s skin might not, in itself, breach the ordinance.
“However, if that conduct forms part of a broader sales strategy involving harassment, coercion or undue influence, it may be relevant,” Yuen said.
Depending on the nature of the physical contact, other criminal issues could also arise, she cautioned.
Amos Cheung, a clinical psychologist registered with the Hong Kong Psychological Society, said falling victim to high-pressure sales tactics did not mean a person was not smart enough.
Such tactics were carefully engineered to exploit human vulnerability and bypass rational reasoning, he said.
Offering free samples could make shoppers feel indebted and reluctant to refuse invitations to enter a store, while applying products to someone’s face without consent could also help identify customers who were more susceptible to manipulation, he said.
Sales representatives could exaggerate imperfections in shoppers’ appearance in ways linked to their self-esteem and sense of self-worth, pushing them towards “emotional reasoning”, Cheung said.
“Such feelings of fear, anxiety and restlessness could impact your rational reasoning process and push you into a state of emotional reasoning,” he said.
He added that compliments could also lower customers’ guard by making sales staff seem friendly and trustworthy.
“If you are unsure about a store’s sales tactics, do not visit it alone,” he said.
“It’s important to be alert to words intended to trigger unnecessary anxiety, shame and panic, and prepare your response, such as ‘I never purchase out of impulse. I will think about it.’ Then, leave immediately.”
*Name changed at interviewee’s request

data.title: Woman found dead in Hong Kong after dog mauling
data.description:
A 33-year-old woman who operated a pet training facility in northern Hong Kong has been found dead after being mauled by a dog, police have said.
Confirming an earlier South China Morning Post report, investigators said closed-circuit television footage showed the woman working alone at the facility at Ping Yeung Tsuen in Ta Kwu Ling when she was attacked by one of the dogs there on Thursday afternoon.
Assistant district commander Matthew Chan Kai-chak of the Border police district said the woman was trying to return a one‑year‑old mongrel to its cage after feeding it in the facility at about 2pm.
The one‑metre-tall dog refused and attacked her for about a minute, leaving wounds on her head, neck, lower jaw and both arms.
A source said the dog could be a mixed breed with pit bull ancestry – a type banned from import and breeding in Hong Kong – and urged the public not to discriminate against mongrels.
CCTV footage showed the woman and the dog leaving the facility and heading towards a lawn area.
Police said they received a report at 4.12pm that a woman had been found collapsed at Ping Yeung Tsuen. She was pronounced dead at the scene.

Chan said the woman was the licence holder of the training centre and dog hotel, which began business at the site in January.
“When officers and paramedics arrived at the scene, the dog was wandering around her body,” Chan said.
Six other dogs were caged when the attack happened. There were no signs of any disturbance at the scene by intruders, police said.
Investigators said volunteers brought the dog to the training centre on August 11 to await adoption.
A postmortem examination will be carried out to establish the cause of death.
Investigators said they had no information on the victim’s health records.
Chan said the training centre was located at No 111 Ping Yeung Tsuen, the address of Pawsgate, a pet facility in Ta Kwu Ling with a 4,500 sq ft grass lawn, a dog swimming pool, indoor play areas and dog boarding and training services.

According to its social media account, the centre provides training services at its premises for dogs that have behaved so badly that they have affected the quality of life of owners for a prolonged period.
It also provides socialising training for dogs that lack interaction with other creatures and easily overreact. The facility also serves as a temporary shelter for stray dogs that people can adopt.
The Labour Department, the Agriculture, Fisheries and Conservation Department, the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (SPCA) and forensic pathologists were at the scene for investigations on Thursday night.
A joint study by the University of Hong Kong and the SPCA in 2021 found that mongrels were the most common victims of animal cruelty in the city.
The incident comes amid citywide concern over the management of large dogs in Hong Kong, after an unleashed 60kg canine fatally attacked two smaller pets on Monday.

data.title: Hong Kong’s rare plot incentive will help resurrect decaying districts: analysts
data.description:
A rare Hong Kong government incentive for developers will help revive old neighbourhoods such as Sham Shui Po, where redevelopment projects have stalled amid a sluggish property market, analysts have said.
They said on Thursday that the bonus plot ratio pilot scheme, due to launch next month, would provide private developers with a financial incentive to redevelop the city’s older neighbourhoods, many of which are plagued by acute urban decay.
Under the scheme, the government will grant developers an extra 20 per cent of gross floor area or an equivalent land premium value in seven urban districts.
Analysts also called for further measures, including a later review of the scheme, adjustments based on market feedback, and an expansion to cover more districts.
“The scheme is equivalent to boosting the site’s redevelopment value by 20 per cent. It serves as a financial incentive that makes redeveloping certain borderline-case old buildings viable,” said lawmaker Augustine Wong Ho-ming, who represents the real estate and construction sector.
He said neighbourhoods such as Sham Shui Po, which have more borderline-case old buildings – ageing properties whose redevelopment feasibility sits on the edge between being financially viable and non-viable – could see faster redevelopment under the scheme than areas like Wan Chai.
Authorities on Wednesday set out the detailed requirements and arrangements of the bonus plot ratio pilot scheme which is intended to expedite private redevelopment in seven old districts.


The seven districts are Cheung Sha Wan, which includes Sham Shui Po; Ma Tau Kok, which covers Kowloon City and To Kwa Wan; Mong Kok; Sai Ying Pun and Sheung Wan; Tsuen Wan; Wan Chai; and Yau Ma Tei.
Under the scheme, a developer that commits to demolishing a residential building aged 50 or above in the seven old districts and redeveloping the site for residential use will be granted an additional 20 per cent premium-free gross floor area as a bonus. The site must have an area of at least 700 square metres (7,534 sq ft).
Developers can choose to submit planning applications to the Town Planning Board, proposing an increase in permissible gross floor area for in situ redevelopment, with a ceiling of 20 per cent. Upon approval, the bonus plot ratio will be premium-free.
If the developer chooses not to increase the gross floor area at the site by up to 20 per cent, the bonus plot ratio can instead be converted into a land premium value.
This value can be used to offset the land premium payable for the developer’s in situ redevelopment project or for other land transactions in the Northern Metropolis and elsewhere in Hong Kong, including land bidding, lease modification or land exchange projects. The land premium value will be valid for 10 years.
The pilot scheme will run for five years, from September 1, 2026 to August 31, 2031.
Tony Wan Wai-ming, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Surveyors, called the scheme an “olive branch” from the government to private developers to boost redevelopment in the city’s old districts.
He said the scheme would offer financial incentives, and the option to convert the bonus plot ratio into a land premium value usable on other land transactions offered flexibility and could encourage developers to launch more projects.
“This is a very flexible approach. For developers with multiple plots of land, it gives them flexibility to make good use of this policy … and it can also encourage them to undertake other projects elsewhere,” he said.
But Wan urged the government to regularly assess the scheme’s implementation and make adjustments, and suggested expanding it to cover more districts to unleash their redevelopment potential.
Lawmaker Wong also called for a review of the scheme at a later stage and its long-term extension to other areas.
Some cases might require a higher bonus ratio and authorities should assess them on a case-by-case basis, he suggested.
Hong Kong is facing acute urban decay. Statistics from the Legislative Council showed that 68.1 per cent of private buildings were aged 30 or above last year. Those aged 50 or above accounted for 25.7 per cent.

Secretary for Development Bernadette Linn Hon-ho said on Wednesday, when the government released details of the pilot scheme, that data over the past decade showed about 20 per cent of the new flats from all redevelopment projects came from the Urban Renewal Authority, with the remaining 80 per cent from private development projects.
“However, as redevelopment projects in old districts involve acquisition costs and there are certain constraints on development parameters for pursuing redevelopment in developed areas, market participation has remained sluggish,” she said.
Lin noted that buildings aged 50 years or above were increasing by more than 500 per year, and would grow by an annual average of more than 700 blocks in the coming 15 years.
“It is necessary for us to adopt an innovative and bolder policy to push the market to undertake redevelopment,” she said.

data.title: Alibaba’s AI cloud growth surge drives earnings despite soaring tech spending
data.description:
Alibaba Group Holding on Thursday reported revenue growth of 45 per cent for its cloud and artificial intelligence division in the June quarter, driving adjusted profit to a better-than-expected 27.3 billion yuan (US$4 billion).
AI Cloud and Compute Services, the Chinese tech giant’s new reporting segment covering its cloud business and T-Head chip arm, posted 48.4 billion yuan in revenue for the three months ended June 30, marking its fastest growth pace in 22 quarters.
The segment’s AI-related product revenue maintained triple-digit growth for the 12th straight quarter, hitting 12.4 billion yuan, up from 8.97 billion yuan in the previous quarter.
Driven by these AI gains, the Hangzhou-based company’s total revenue increased 9 per cent year on year to 269 billion yuan for the quarter, in line with the Bloomberg consensus estimate of 268.5 billion yuan. That was faster than the 3 per cent growth seen in the previous quarter.
Adjusted Ebitda – earnings before interest, taxes and amortisation, and a measure of profitability – dropped by 30 per cent year on year to 27.3 billion yuan, compared with the analyst consensus forecast of 26.6 billion yuan.
Capital expenditure also surged 75 per cent from a year earlier to 67.7 billion yuan, compared with 26.9 billion yuan recorded in the previous quarter.
Free cash outflow in the reported quarter more than doubled to 44.7 billion yuan from 18.8 billion yuan a year earlier, as heavier investment in cloud infrastructure further strained cash generation.
Alibaba’s New York-listed shares slid 4 per cent in pre-market trading following the earnings announcement. Its Hong Kong-listed shares gained 1.6 per cent to HK$126.2 on Thursday, ahead of the release.
The results underscore Alibaba’s strategy of building full-stack AI capabilities – from chips and models to applications – as it seeks to cement its position as a market leader amid intense domestic and international competition.
During the June quarter, the company streamlined its reporting segments in a “strategic alignment” designed to better integrate its commerce and AI businesses. They now report under four main units: Alibaba E-commerce Group, AI Cloud and Compute Services, AI Labs and Applications, and others.

The AI Labs and Applications division – covering its AI model labs, Qwen Consumer Business Group and workplace AI agent platform QwenWork – generated 3,338 million yuan in revenue, a 16 per cent year-on-year increase.
“We delivered a strong quarter, driven by the improving commercialisation of our full‑stack AI capabilities,” said Eddie Wu Yongming, CEO of Alibaba Group, which owns the South China Morning Post.
The company’s full‑stack strategy has put it “in a superior position to capture the substantial growth of demand for artificial intelligence and AI compute”, he said.
Meanwhile, Alibaba E-commerce Group, which combines domestic and international e-commerce operations along with grocery chain Freshippo, recorded a 4 per cent year-on-year revenue increase to 205.9 billion yuan, with an adjusted Ebitda of 39.7 billion yuan.

data.title: Why do hard-sell beauty tactics persist – and when can consumers fight back?
data.description:
From arrests linked to the Hong Kong operations of beauty chain Opatra London to a surge in online complaints against other skincare brands, high-pressure sales tactics remain widespread and continue to take a toll on consumers.
Why do such malpractices remain widespread despite the city’s Trade Descriptions Ordinance, which criminalises aggressive commercial practices that significantly impair a consumer’s freedom of choice?
The South China Morning Post spoke to legal experts about common hard-sell scenarios, how shoppers can protect themselves and where the legal line is drawn.
1. Paid to escape? You can still report it
Lawyers say sales encounters without any physical contact can still amount to an offence, as courts could rule that a consumer’s freedom of choice was “significantly impaired” in such scenarios.
“The question is whether the conduct as a whole amounted to harassment, coercion or undue influence that significantly impaired the consumer’s freedom of choice and caused the consumer to make a purchase that he or she would not otherwise have made,” commercial lawyer Kenix Yuen Pui-kwan told the SCMP.
Lawyer Eric Chan Pak-ho said “undue influence” under the law means exploiting one’s position of power over the consumer to apply pressure, without needing to use or threaten physical force.

2. Card snatched or held? That’s likely an offence
Chan described this as a “classic case” of an aggressive commercial practice.
He said snatching a customer’s credit card to conduct a transaction and holding on to a customer’s card after they decline to purchase were typical examples of coercion and undue influence under the ordinance.
3. Products applied without consent: not always illegal, but can count
This act may not breach the law, but lawyers say it can contribute to an overall assessment of whether an aggressive commercial practice occurred.
Chan added that such conduct could also increase the culpability of a prosecuted firm.
Yuen said if the unsolicited application of products caused the consumer to make a purchase they otherwise would not have made, it could fall within the scope of the law.
“For example, if the unsolicited application of products is used to create pressure, embarrassment or discomfort, and thereby causes the consumer to make a purchase that they would not otherwise have made, the conduct could potentially fall within the scope of an aggressive commercial practice,” Yuen said.

4. Trapped in a room or free to walk out? It matters in court
It can be highly relevant as evidence of whether it was easy for the consumer to disengage from the sales practice, according to lawyers.
Aggressive commercial practices can occur in both enclosed locations, such as beauty treatment rooms, and open-door store spaces, such as shops inside a shopping centre.
Yuen said an enclosed treatment or consultation room – or a gym – might make it easier to establish that the consumer was placed under sustained pressure or could not leave freely.
“Conversely, in an open-door shop within a shopping centre, a consumer may generally have greater practical freedom to walk away, although an aggressive commercial practice may still occur if the sales tactics are sufficiently persistent, intimidating or coercive,” Yuen said.
5. Have courts convicted salons for hard-sell tactics?
Although cases involving aggressive commercial practices can face evidentiary hurdles – such as conflicting accounts between the consumer and staff, and the absence of independent witnesses – there have been convictions.
In 2015, three saleswomen at a beauty salon were convicted under the ordinance for badgering a woman for an hour and a half inside the parlour to purchase HK$140,000 (US$17,852) worth of body-care treatments.
One of the women told the customer there was a lump in her breast, before she and her colleagues intensely persuaded her to buy the treatment package.
Two of the saleswomen were sentenced to three months’ imprisonment, while another received a community service order.
But an SCMP search of the judiciary’s judgments database found fewer than 10 judgments or sentencing-reasons documents in cases involving aggressive commercial practices.
